transcript:
This message comes from Mattress Firm.
Restless partner keeping you up?
Mattress Firm's sleep experts can match you with a Tempur-Pedic that absorbs motion.
Get a $300 instant gift toward a Tempur-Pedic total sleep solution with Mattress Purchase.
They make sleep easy.
As NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports, these show that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political block has lost its majority in Parliament.
Both Netanyahu's block and the main opposition failed to secure the 61 seats in the Israeli Parliament needed to form a government.
What follows are complex negotiations and horse-trading as each side tries to build the coalition it needs to reach a majority.
A key question is whether the center-right opposition will partner with Arab-led parties who won a record 19 seats in this election.
Since the October 7th Hamas attacks on Israel three years ago, Arab leaders have been demonized in Israel.
But partnering with them is one route to unseat Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, Ruth Sherlock, NPR News Tel Aviv.
Meanwhile, Iran continues to target ships that are attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shelchi reports from Istanbul, this comes as the United States and Israel prepare for a potential return to hostilities in the Middle East.
The Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that in the past 24 hours, three oil tankers struck mines it had previously set up as they tried to exit the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media.
It reported that the vessels were going through a "unauthorized route" and that the ships caught fire. There were no reports of casualties.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations, which monitors shipping vessels, said that October had the highest number of attacks in the straits since the beginning of the war.
The monitoring group elevated the regional threat level to "severe" due to the volume of strikes.
The US has been escorting some oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, even with the spike of Iranian strikes.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
The Justice Department has issued grand jury subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles County.
NPR's Jude Jaffee Block reports on what appears to be the Trump administration's escalation of a feud over California voter rolls ahead of next week's midterm elections.
The Los Angeles County Registrar/Recorder's Office confirmed it received grand jury subpoenas last week.
It's unclear at this point whether the employees who were subpoenaed are the targets of the criminal probe.
But federal prosecutors have warned California election officials they could be committing a crime if they process ballots cast by non-citizens.
The Justice Department is trying to force California to set aside the ballots of people federal officials say are likely non-citizens.
But a federal judge rejected that request this week. The Justice Department has appealed.
The same judge also told federal prosecutors to stop threatening local officials.
Jude Jaffee Block, NPR News.
This is NPR.
President Trump's campaign plans have been adapted for this weekend.
He was supposed to make in-person trips to rallies in Iowa and Kansas.
Instead, Republican National Committee officials say that Trump will phone into nearly 20 rallies around the country to support Republican candidates.
He will still stump today in Florida.
The GOP officials say the president's plans changed because Republican candidates are doing well.
But Democrats have expressed doubt, citing President Trump's low approval ratings.
The biggest cryptocurrency exchange in the world, Binance, says it's suspended withdrawals.
It also revealed thieves have stolen more than $6 billion from the company.
Halloween is just around the corner, and the cost of handing out candy is not getting any cheaper.
And Piers Joe Hernandez reports on the rising cost of chocolate and other sweets.
According to the latest federal data, prices for candy and gum are up 7.7 percent in one year and more than 18 percent in two years.
One major culprit is chocolate after drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons.
Global cocoa production is rebounding, but consumer chocolate prices remain elevated, and shoppers are pulling back.
That's according to data from Circana, which tracks sales in supermarkets across the U.S.
They found that people have been buying less chocolate each year for several years running,
but dollar sales are up, which means people are spending more money on chocolate but getting less of it.
Joe Hernandez, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
